did.abstract: Unit within the office of the Vice President for Student Life of the University of Michigan that began its history as a counseling information clearinghouse and later assumed responsibility for direct mental health counseling of students. Records include minutes from various committees, topical files covering CAPS initiatives related to campus mental health, reports created by CAPS' predecessor office Counseling Services, service and demographic data, published resources, and director's files.

acqinfo.p: The record group (Donor 8128) was received beginning in 1993. Further records donated July 2024. Periodic accessions are expected.

p.emph: Access Restrictions for University of Michigan Records

blockquote.p: University records are public records and once fully processed are generally open to research use. Records that contain personally identifiable information will be restricted in order to protect individual privacy. Certain administrative records are restricted in accordance with university policy as outlined below. The restriction of university records is subject to compliance with applicable laws, including the Michigan Freedom of Information Act.

Categories of Restricted Records
Executive records: Records generated by the university's executive officers, deans, directors, department heads, and their designated support staff are restricted for twenty (20) years from the date of their creation.
Restricted files are indicated in the contents list of the collection’s finding aid with a restriction note indicating the restriction type and the date of expiration.

For further information on the restriction policy and placing Freedom of Information Act requests for restricted material, consult the reference archivist at the Bentley Historical Library (bentley.ref@umich.edu) or the University of Michigan Freedom of Information Office website (https://foia.vpcomm.umich.edu/).

bioghist.p: Counseling and Psychological Services was established at the University of Michigan in 1961 as the Coordinator of Counseling Services position, part of the creation of the new Office of Student Affairs. The Coordinator's office assisted students in obtaining non-academic information and oversaw the release of student information to non-university agencies—it did not provide individual counseling or mental health services directly. In the Faculty and Staff Guide to Counseling and Student Services, which was published by the University Committee on Student Counseling Services from 1964-1977, the function of the Office of the Coordinator of Counseling was characterized as "the chief clearinghouse of counseling information, not a clinical agency." [1969/70 Guide to Counseling and Student Services, p. 16]

During the 1965/66 academic year, the office of the Vice President for Student Affairs was reorganized. A Student Affairs Counseling Office was created in 1967, incorporating the Counseling Division of the Bureau of Psychological Services. Edward S. Bordin, chief of Counseling Division, was named Director of the Counseling Office and remained so through 1973. Elizabeth Davenport served as assistant director from 1965 until 1969/70.

The 1970s was a decade of evolution for counseling at the University, beginning with another reorganization of the Office of the Vice President for Student Affairs in academic year 1970/71, during which the Counseling Office became Counseling Services (CS). Counseling Services' main responsibilities included coordinating direct counseling services with the Mental Health Clinic, providing consultation to university faculty and staff, creating and coordinating educational programming, and researching campus and community mental health.

Throughout the early 1970s, direct counseling services added increased services for marginalized student populations, such as Black Information Counseling (BIC), and expanded consultation services to the Housing Office. The Educational Programming and Consultation (EPC) program included teaching services in the Psychology Department, graduate intern training, sex education, and the Drug Education Project. The 76-GUIDE, a 24/7 telephone hotline staffed by peer counselors with support from CS, opened and began providing counseling, problem solving, referral, and rumor control.

During the 1974/75 academic year Counseling Services merged with the Mental Health Clinic of University Health Services. The two together retained the name of Counseling Services. As a result of this merger, the major focus of Counseling Services shifted over the next five years from a coordinating office and information clearinghouse to direct counseling of individuals, couples and groups in matters such as mental health management, academic stress, pregnancy, marital relations, sexuality, and marginalized community concerns. During the 1978/79 academic year, the office implemented daily professional staff teams to provide students with immediate walk-in service. In the 1980s, CS added the Human Sexuality Office and the Sexual Assault Crisis Center (later the Sexual Assault Prevention and Awareness Center [SAPAC]).

In 1982/83, the office set up its first data management system to document the number of individuals using counseling services and to provide complete and updated information on services delivered. The office added an in-house psychiatrist position in 1992 and worked continuously to lower wait-times for students. In 1994, the name was changed to Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS) to better reflect its role at the university. Throughout the 1990s, CAPS engaged in outreach to specific areas of the university, such as international students, the Law School, and Athletics, offering tailored services for unique mental health needs.

The 21st century saw CAPS fully emerge as a leading-edge university counseling center. In 2001, CAPS staff psychologists developed the Counseling Center Assessment of Psychological Symptoms (CCAPS), a mental health screening tool specifically for college students that is still widely used in the field. Under director Todd Sevig, who assumed the position in 2001, CAPS created the College Student Mental Health Survey, which has provided over two decades of data on mental health on college campuses. Sevig's tenure also saw the creation of the embedded model of counseling, in which individual counselors are embedded in U-M schools and colleges, as well as the opening of three Wellness Zones that offer a place for students to practice emotional wellness and stress management.

Today CAPS shapes U-M's student mental health messaging as part of the Office of Student Life, creating policies and resources such as the University's Psychiatric Withdrawal Policy and a Guide to Mental Health Hospitalization for students. The office currently focuses on direct individual and group counseling, drop-in services, outreach and trainings, and fighting stigma around mental health services. In 2024, it merged with the University Health Service and is housed administratively under the unit University Health & Counseling.

chronlist.head: Directors of Counseling and Psychological Services

scopecontent.p: The records of Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS) provide a unique look at the response of the university to the non-academic needs of the student body. The records cover the origin and creation of Counseling Services (CS) at the University of Michigan and track the evolution of the office as it transitioned from a supplier of counseling information to offering direct mental health counseling and outreach services to students. The materials include minutes from various committees, topical files covering CS/CAPS initiatives related to campus mental health, reports created by CAPS and Counseling Services, service and demographic data, the Campus Mental Health Survey data and reports, published resources, and administrative files.

arrangement.p: The records are arranged in 5 series: 1. Minutes 2. Topical Files 3. Reports 4. Director's Files 5. Publications

relatedmaterial.p: The Bentley Historical Library houses the following related collections: Vice President for Student Life (University of Michigan) records.
Additional publications from COunseling Services, including annual reports, can be found in University of Michigan assorted publications, circa 1920-2016.

scopecontent.p: The Minutes Series consists of minutes from the various committees related to Counseling Services. The Staff Meeting minutes and the Coordinating Council minutes provide the best documentation of the overall scope of the Counseling Services office. Within the weekly minutes of these two committees, the researcher will find reports of the various programs and committees operating within the Counseling Office. The minutes of the Advisory and Policy of Care Committees illustrate the various ethical and operational questions confronting the staff in their attempt to meet the needs of the ever-changing student body. Lastly, the minutes of the University Committee on Student Counseling Services document the earliest years of counseling, the Office of the Coordinator of Counseling.

did.unittitle: University Committee on Student Counseling Services

scopecontent.p: The Topical Files are arranged alphabetically and document the various services and programs available to students. The overall functions of Counseling Services are best described within the "General," Goal Statements," and "Objectives" folders. The "Annual Report Background Files" contain the reports submitted from various programs within Counseling that were used in the preparation of the Annual Report to the President.

The "Student Survey on Counseling" files include the 1956 survey conducted by the Counseling Study Committee of the University of Michigan. The survey was conducted to examine student attitudes about the available counseling services on campus. As a result of this survey the 1958 publication, A Guide to the Resources for Student Counseling and Advising at the University of Michigan was created. This publication is the predecessor of the Guide to Counseling, published by Counseling Services in the 1960s and 1970s. In addition to the Guide, a statement of goals was written for a university-wide counseling program. The Counseling Services Office was an outgrowth of this goal statement.

The records in this series also document programs created to meet the needs of the student body. The 76-Guide files give evidence of the 24-hour referral and information service sponsored by Counseling Office that started as an experiment in the lobby of the Student Activities Building. This unique counseling service, which was staffed by student peer counselors supported by counselors at CS, provided immediate counseling and referral, as well as serving as a central hotline for campus rumor control.

The Educational Programming and Consultation Unit files relate this out-reach branch of counseling, which is responsible for creating and implementing programs to assist other university units. The researcher will find proposals, program modules and written objectives within the EP&C files. Additionally, there is information on two of the most popular programs: the Housing Consultation project, a program to support residence hall staff in their work with students; and the Peer Development program, a program allowing trained students to counsel their peers.

scopecontent.p: The Director's Files series covers the administrative, clinical, and research activities of Counseling Services (later Counseling and Psychological Services) from the late 1970s through the 2020s. The records came from former director Todd Sevig, who served as director from 2001-2024, but cover the tenures of directors Harold Korn, James Whiteside, A. Delories Sloan, Millie Tirado, and Sevig. Included are records documenting CS/CAPS' initiatives related to substance abuse, sexual assualt, eating disorders, suicide prevention, student mental health hospitalization, and expanding services to North Campus and family housing. Also included are long range studies and reports created, commissioned by, or supported by CS/CAPS, including reports on campus climate for LGBTQ students, reports from the Mental Health Work Group on how to best meet student mental health needs, client satisfcation surveys, and data submitted to yearly surveys run by other universities. These, along with extensive demographic summaries and service self-assessments offer a very comprehensive picture of the evolution of CS/CAPS and its services.
The files are arranged alphabetically. There is some subject overlap among these files with those found in the Topical Files and Reports series.
